answers.primary: A dynamic workflow: Claude writes a JavaScript orchestration script that discovers the route handler files, runs pipeline() to spawn one auditor agent per file, and then feeds each candidate finding to an adversarial verifier stage before anything is reported. After the first good run, press s in /workflows to save the script to .claude/workflows/ so it becomes a project command that reruns the same orchestration next quarter.
answers.rejected_alternative: Fanning out subagents turn by turn from the main conversation, rejected because Claude re-decides the plan every turn, 400 per-file results would land in one context window, and the orchestration itself is not a reusable artifact.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. The workflow runtime executes the script, so the per-file fan-out, the verification stage and the ordering between them are code rather than model judgment. The model still owns the quality of each individual audit and each verification verdict.
answers.context_boundary: Each auditor and verifier runs in its own agent context, and intermediate findings live in script variables inside the isolated workflow runtime, not in the session. Only the final filtered report crosses back into the conversation, along with the path of the script that was run.
answers.lifecycle: It runs when you invoke the saved command, or when you ask for a workflow with the ultracode keyword, and it runs in the background while the session stays responsive. It stops when the script returns, when you stop it from /workflows, or when it hits the 1,000 agent per run cap; a run is resumable only within the same session.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open and is advisory: a workflow is orchestration, not a gate, so an authorization hole that no auditor notices is simply never reported and nothing blocks the quarter from being declared clean. Practically, stopping mid fan-out is expensive because replay re-runs every agent that started after the first unfinished one, and a 400 file run only earns an advisory Large workflow warning rather than a stop.
answers.version_caveat: Dynamic workflows require Claude Code v2.1.154 or later and a paid plan (on Pro they must be turned on from the Dynamic workflows row in /config), and an organization can kill them with disableWorkflows in managed settings. From v2.1.219 the default size guideline is medium, meaning Claude aims for fewer than 15 agents, so a 400 file fan-out needs the guideline raised; saving to the project location refuses to write through symlinks as of v2.1.216.

answers.primary: An agent team: spawn five teammates from the lead session, each assigned one hypothesis in its spawn prompt, with instructions to message each other and try to disprove each other's theories, and to write whatever consensus survives into a findings document on disk that the lead synthesizes at the end.
answers.rejected_alternative: Parallel subagents, rejected because subagents only report results back to the main agent and can never message each other, so the adversarial debate that is the entire point of this design cannot happen.
answers.enforcement_owner: The model. The lead decides who investigates what and when the debate is finished, and each teammate decides what to challenge; the harness only supplies the mailbox files, the shared task list, and file locking on task claims.
answers.context_boundary: Every teammate is a full independent Claude Code session with its own context window that loads project CLAUDE.md, skills and MCP servers but not the lead's conversation history. What crosses the boundary is the spawn prompt, SendMessage messages between named agents, shared task list entries, idle notifications to the lead, and the findings document on disk.
answers.lifecycle: The team forms when the first teammate is spawned after you approve, and teammates run until they go idle, are asked to shut down, or the session ends. The team config directory is removed automatically at session exit while the task list persists, and in-process teammates are not restored by /resume or /rewind.
answers.failure_mode: Advisory and fails open: nothing forces the teammates to actually argue or to converge, the lead can declare the investigation finished before the work is done, teammates sometimes stop on errors or forget to mark tasks complete, and the surviving consensus is what five agents agreed on rather than a verified root cause. Token cost scales linearly with five separate context windows.
answers.version_caveat: Agent teams are experimental and disabled by default; nothing is set up unless CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1 is set in settings.json or the environment. The documented behavior is as of v2.1.178, where TeamCreate and TeamDelete no longer exist and cleanup is automatic; before v2.1.207 one malformed mailbox entry blocked delivery for that agent, and from v2.1.198 a teammate whose turn dies on an API error tells the lead it failed instead of appearing to finish.

answers.primary: A subagent: delegate the suite run to a test-runner subagent defined in .claude/agents/ with Bash plus read-only search tools and a system prompt that says to report only failing tests and their error messages. The tens of thousands of lines stay in the subagent's own context window and only its final summary returns.
answers.rejected_alternative: A skill holding the same instructions, rejected because a skill runs in the main conversation context, so the raw suite output would land in the very window you are trying to protect.
answers.enforcement_owner: Split, and worth being honest about: the harness owns the context isolation, because a subagent gets a fresh isolated context and a separate transcript file and only its final report is returned. The model owns the filtering, so the promise that only failures come back is an instruction, not a guarantee.
answers.context_boundary: The subagent starts with its own system prompt, the delegation message, CLAUDE.md and a git status snapshot, and it does not see your conversation history. The raw stdout lives only in its context and its transcript file under the session directory; only the final report crosses back, after subagent output scanning.
answers.lifecycle: It runs each time Claude delegates to it, by description match or @-mention, and ends when it returns its report. The definition file persists on disk and is hot-reloaded within seconds of an edit; a finished instance can be resumed later with SendMessage.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open on the thing you care about second: the isolation holds, but nothing stops the subagent from pasting large blocks of raw output into its summary or from silently truncating or mis-summarizing failures. If the run is cut off by an API error you get partial output with a note, and a background subagent's result only reaches Claude as a completion notification in a later turn.
answers.version_caveat: As of v2.1.198 subagents run in the background by default and background subagents get a reduced built-in tool set (Bash, Read, Grep, Glob, Edit, Write and a few others survive), so a definition can resolve to different tools in foreground and background; set CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_BACKGROUND_TASKS=1 to keep it synchronous. Also from v2.1.198 /agents no longer opens a creation wizard, so write the file or ask Claude to; output scanning of the returned report requires v2.1.210 or later.

answers.primary: An agent team of three teammates, one owning the frontend, one the backend API and one the test suite, with the file ownership partitioned explicitly in each spawn prompt and the evolving interface contract communicated between them over SendMessage and the shared task list.
answers.rejected_alternative: Subagents, rejected because they cannot message each other as the contract changes and you cannot address one of them directly; every instruction would have to be relayed through the main agent.
answers.enforcement_owner: The model. The lead assigns and supervises, and each teammate decides when to tell the others the interface changed; the harness only provides the mailbox, the shared task list with dependency tracking, and file-locked task claiming.
answers.context_boundary: Each teammate has its own context window and loads the project's CLAUDE.md, skills and MCP servers, but not the lead's history. What crosses is the spawn prompt, direct messages by teammate name, task list state, plan approval requests, idle notifications, and anything written to shared files in the repository.
answers.lifecycle: It starts when you ask for teammates and confirm, and each teammate runs until it goes idle or is shut down by name; the team is scoped to the session and cleaned up when the session ends. There is one team per session, no nesting, and the lead cannot be transferred.
answers.failure_mode: Advisory and fails open in the most dangerous way for cross-layer work: agent teams do not isolate teammates in worktrees, so two teammates touching the same file overwrite each other, and the only defense is that you partitioned the files correctly up front. Interface drift is also unenforced, since a teammate that forgets to announce a contract change simply breaks the others' assumptions.
answers.version_caveat: Experimental and off unless CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1 is set. Dropping into a worker directly depends on the display mode: the default has been in-process since v2.1.179 (arrow keys then Enter in the agent panel), while split panes need tmux or iTerm2 with the it2 CLI and are unsupported in the VS Code integrated terminal, Windows Terminal and Ghostty. Teammate permission prompts surface in the lead session, and permission modes cannot be set per teammate at spawn time.

answers.primary: A dynamic workflow: ask for a workflow that runs the strict type check, dispatches agents to fix the reported errors, and repeats, with the loop and the stop condition (clean run, or two consecutive rounds with no reduction in errors) written into the script rather than re-decided in conversation.
answers.rejected_alternative: A skill that instructs Claude to keep looping, rejected because with a skill Claude holds the plan and re-evaluates continuation every round in the main context, which is exactly the babysitting and re-deciding you asked to eliminate.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. The workflow runtime executes the loop, the comparison between rounds and the termination test as code; the model only owns each round's diagnosis and edits.
answers.context_boundary: The script runs in an isolated runtime separate from your conversation, and each round's type checker output stays in the fixing agents' contexts and in script variables. Only the final outcome, whether it passed or stalled, reaches your session.
answers.lifecycle: It starts on invocation and runs in the background until the script's exit condition trips, you stop it from /workflows, or it hits the runtime caps. Resume works within the same session only; exiting Claude Code makes the next session start it fresh.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open. The runtime takes no mid-run user input, so a badly written stop condition just keeps burning rounds until you notice, and the workflow's agents always run in acceptEdits regardless of your session mode, so silencing fixes such as blanket any casts get applied without review. A green type check at the end is not evidence the code is better.
answers.version_caveat: Requires Claude Code v2.1.154 or later and a paid plan, with Pro users enabling it in /config. Note that shell commands not already in your allowlist can still prompt mid-run, so allowlist the type check command before starting an unattended loop, and that the ultracode keyword only opts you in when you type it yourself, not from -p, a scheduled task, or a relayed webhook prompt.

answers.primary: A dynamic workflow: one discovery agent lists the component files, pipeline() runs one transform agent per file with each agent working in its own isolated copy of the repository (worktree isolation), and a verification agent checks each transformed file before the item counts as done.
answers.rejected_alternative: Subagents with isolation: worktree driven turn by turn by Claude, rejected because roughly 500 items outgrows what one conversation can coordinate and the per-file results would fill the main context long before the migration finished.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness for the structure: the runtime executes the fan-out, the isolation and the ordering of transform then verify. The model owns whether each rewritten component is actually correct and whether a verifier is being honest about it.
answers.context_boundary: Every file's diff, build output and verification reasoning stays inside that agent's own context and in script variables in the workflow runtime. Only the aggregate result crosses into your conversation; the isolated copies exist on disk and their changes must be brought back explicitly.
answers.lifecycle: It runs on invocation and in the background until the pipeline drains. It is resumable in the same session, but the replay rule means every agent that started after the first unfinished one re-runs, which is why many small per-file agents preserve more progress than one long agent.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open: verified means an agent asserted the result looked right, not that anything gated it. Scale is the practical trap, since the runtime allows only 16 concurrent agents and 1,000 agents per run, so 500 files times a transform plus a verify plus discovery sits close to the ceiling, and the cost of a full run is large enough that you should trial it on one directory first.
answers.version_caveat: Workflows require v2.1.154 or later on a paid plan. If you implement the isolation with the subagent isolation: worktree field, note that from v2.1.203 the agent's Bash and PowerShell commands must resolve inside its worktree or they fail, and from v2.1.216 Bash commands that redirect git into the main checkout (git -C, --git-dir, GIT_DIR, or a cd) fail as well; a worktree whose agent made no changes is cleaned up automatically.

answers.primary: A dynamic workflow: pipeline() spawns one reviewer agent per changed file, and a single synthesis agent then receives all per-file findings and merges, deduplicates and ranks them into one summary. Save the script as a command so the same review runs on every branch.
answers.rejected_alternative: An agent team, rejected because the reviewers have nothing to say to each other, so the mailbox, shared task list and per-teammate context windows are pure coordination overhead and token cost for no benefit.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness owns the shape: the script guarantees one reviewer per file and that exactly one merge stage runs afterward. The model owns review quality and the judgment calls inside the deduplication and ranking.
answers.context_boundary: Sixty sets of per-file findings live in script variables and in each reviewer's own context; the merge agent receives them from the script, and only its single ranked summary crosses into your conversation.
answers.lifecycle: It runs per invocation, in the background, and ends when the merge agent returns. As a saved command it applies to whatever diff you point it at and stops applying the moment you stop invoking it.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open and is advisory. The structure itself creates a blind spot: a reviewer that sees only its own file cannot see a defect that spans two files, and the merge agent can drop real findings while deduplicating near-identical ones. Nothing prevents the PR from merging if the summary is empty.
answers.version_caveat: Requires v2.1.154 or later on a paid plan. The default size guideline has been medium since v2.1.219, which advises Claude toward fewer than 15 agents and will fight a 60 agent fan-out unless you set workflowSizeGuideline to large or unrestricted; a run scheduling more than 25 agents also shows the advisory Large workflow warning in the task panel from v2.1.203.

answers.primary: Chained subagents in the main conversation: three project subagent definitions in .claude/agents/, a read-only performance analyst (Read, Grep, Glob, Bash), an optimizer that also has Edit, and a verifier, invoked one after another so Claude passes each one's returned findings into the next one's prompt.
answers.rejected_alternative: An agent team, rejected because the work is strictly sequential, every step depends on the previous one, and all three touch the same handful of files, which is precisely the case where teammates overwrite each other and a single session with subagents is the better fit.
answers.enforcement_owner: The model. Claude decides the order, decides what to hand forward, and decides that the verifier runs at all; the harness only enforces each definition's tool allowlist, so the read-only analyst genuinely cannot edit. If the sequence must be guaranteed rather than intended, move it into a workflow script and the harness owns it.
answers.context_boundary: Each subagent starts with a fresh isolated context containing its own system prompt, the delegation message, CLAUDE.md and a git status snapshot. The handoff between stages goes through the main conversation as a summary, not as a transcript, so what stage two receives is what Claude chose to restate.
answers.lifecycle: Each subagent runs on delegation within the turn and ends when it returns its result. The definitions persist on disk and are picked up on the next delegation after an edit; an individual instance can be resumed with SendMessage if you need it to continue rather than start over.
answers.failure_mode: Advisory and fails open. Nothing stops Claude from skipping the verifier, reordering the steps, or letting the optimizer fix things nobody found, and the summarized handoff is lossy enough that the fixer may not receive the exact list of findings. Because all three work the same hot files, they must run strictly one at a time; running any two concurrently risks clobbering edits.
answers.version_caveat: As of v2.1.198 subagents run in the background by default and their results arrive as a completion notification in a later turn (behavior tightened in v2.1.211), which is awkward for a strict chain; ask for foreground runs or set CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_BACKGROUND_TASKS=1. Background runs also see a reduced built-in tool set, and there is a 200 subagent per session cap from v2.1.212 and a 20 concurrent cap from v2.1.217.

answers.primary: An agent team of three teammates, one on user experience, one on technical architecture and one playing devil's advocate, told in their spawn prompts to message each other and react to the arguments as they form, with the lead synthesizing the design decision at the end.
answers.rejected_alternative: A dynamic workflow that drafts the design from several angles and weighs them against each other, rejected because a workflow run takes no mid-run user input, so you could not jump into one explorer mid-flight and redirect it.
answers.enforcement_owner: The model. The lead spawns, names and synthesizes, and the explorers decide what to challenge; the harness contributes the mailbox, the agent panel and the shared task list.
answers.context_boundary: Each explorer is a separate session with its own context window loading project CLAUDE.md, skills and MCP servers but not the lead's history. Crossing the boundary: the spawn prompt, inter-teammate messages, the messages you type directly into a teammate's transcript, and the findings the lead pulls together.
answers.lifecycle: It starts when you request the team and confirm, and each explorer runs until it goes idle or you shut it down by name; the team is scoped to this session and its config directory is removed when the session ends.
answers.failure_mode: Advisory. The debate is a prompt, not a mechanism, so three teammates can converge on the same comfortable answer; the lead may synthesize before the exploration is finished; and token usage is roughly three independent sessions. An explorer whose row disappeared has only been hidden after going idle, which reads as a crash if you do not know the rule.
answers.version_caveat: Experimental and requires CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1. Redirecting one explorer works in the default in-process mode by selecting its row and pressing Enter, but while you are viewing a teammate built-in slash commands still run in the lead's session, and /model and /fast only ever change the lead (from v2.1.199 you at least get a notice); idle row hiding changed in v2.1.181 and again in v2.1.199.

answers.primary: Nested subagents: one reviewer subagent that keeps the Agent tool in its tools list, so it reviews the recent changes and then dispatches its own verifier subagent per finding. Only the reviewer's single final summary returns to your conversation.
answers.rejected_alternative: A dynamic workflow, rejected because 5 to 10 findings is well inside what one delegated agent can coordinate, and a workflow adds an approval prompt, a background runtime and a script artifact for a job that a single nested delegation already isolates.
answers.enforcement_owner: Split: the harness owns the boundary, since a nested subagent's output can only reach its parent and only the top-level subagent's summary returns to the main conversation. The model owns the discipline of actually dispatching one independent verifier per finding rather than checking its own work.
answers.context_boundary: Two layers run below your session. The reviewer's tool calls and every verifier's transcript stay in their own context windows, and the verifier verdicts reach only the reviewer. Exactly one report crosses into your conversation, after subagent output scanning.
answers.lifecycle: It runs when you delegate the review and ends when the reviewer returns its summary. Nesting is bounded by the spawn depth limit; at the limit the Agent tool is withheld and the agent must finish the work itself.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open, and the specific failure is quiet: if the depth limit is reached, the reviewer simply loses the Agent tool and verifies its own findings, collapsing independent verification into self-review with no error you would notice in the summary. The 20 concurrent and 200 per session subagent caps also apply, and a verifier cut off by an API error returns partial output.
answers.version_caveat: The depth limit is version-sensitive: v2.1.172 through v2.1.216 nested up to five layers with no way to change it, v2.1.217 and v2.1.218 defaulted to one layer so this pattern did not work at all, and v2.1.219 raised the default to three with CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH available from v2.1.217 to tune it. Subagent output scanning of the returned report requires v2.1.210 or later.
